newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - SAB beer strong, subsidiaries weak.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - SAB beer strong, subsidiaries weak.

text.p: Bubbling offshore beer sales coupled with a modest increase in local volumes is expected to cheer year earnings at South African Breweries Ltd (SAB), the world's fourth biggest brewer.

But analysts said on Wednesday disappointing performances at heavyweight subsidiaries, Edgars Stores Ltd and Plate Glass & Shatterprufe Industries Ltd, will confine profits, due to be reported next Tuesday, to a moderate rise.
"We will see fairly poor results from Edgars and Plate Glass. They are dragging it down," said Tom de Trafford, an analyst at Simpson McKie James Capel.

Analysts polled by Reuters forecast SAB's fully diluted earnings per share for the year to March 31 rising to between 599.0 and 630.8 cents a share with consensus at 617.8 -- 14.2 percent up on last year's 540.8 cents and equalling the growth at half year.
They predicted a dividend of between 280.0 and 290.0 cents with expectations averaging out at 286.3 from 250.0 a year ago.
Edgars this week reported year attributable earnings down five percent to 320.9 million rand amid a squeeze on margins and only a slim increase in volumes.
Plate Glass reports results for the year to end-March on Friday. Analysts have forecast earnings per share falling to between 689.1 and 707.5 cents from 745.0 cents a year ago.
SAB retail unit OK Bazaars, which has been delisted from the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, was also expected to perform badly.
"OK Bazaars could be a disaster. They could lose as much as 80 million rand," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.

Pedestrian profits from these subsidiaries already at the halfway stage led SAB deputy chairman, Selwyn McFarlane, to say that the firm's non-beer interests might be "reshuffled" if they did not manage to compete on international terms.

But robust volume growth of around 25 percent in beer sales at its overseas operations -- SAB is the largest brewer in Poland, Hungary and Romania and owns breweries in several African countries -- would help earnings growth.
Local beer sales, where SAB has a near monopoly, were seen rising a more pedestrian 15 percent year-on-year.

"The international operations will surprise on the upside. I think people are underestimating them...The biggest factor will be the low finance costs following last year's equity issue," another analyst said.

SAB last year launched a $413 million international share issue to raise funds for its overseas expansion. The group is mulling further drives into Eastern Europe, notably Bulgaria, as well as into Russia, Latin America and East Africa.
